blockMcqs.question: What does a replacement policy decide?
options: Which cache line to evict when a set is full
How big the cache line is
blockMcqs.explanation: Replacement policy picks the eviction victim; write policy handles when memory is updated.

blockMcqs.question: LRU evicts which line from a full set?
blockMcqs.explanation: LRU tracks use order and evicts whichever line has gone longest without an access.

blockMcqs.question: When does write-back update main memory?
options: Only when the line is evicted
blockMcqs.explanation: Write-back delays memory updates until eviction, tracked via the dirty bit.

blockMcqs.question: A miss from too many addresses sharing a set is which C?
blockMcqs.explanation: Conflict misses happen when addresses collide in the same set despite free space elsewhere.

blockMcqs.question: AMAT is computed as which formula?
options: Hit time + miss rate × miss penalty
blockMcqs.explanation: AMAT adds the guaranteed hit time to the expected cost of misses (rate times penalty).

blockMcqs.question: Raising associativity mainly reduces which misses?
blockMcqs.explanation: More ways per set give colliding addresses more places to land, cutting conflict misses.

blockMcqs.question: Why not just make every cache huge?
options: Larger caches are slower and costlier per byte
Cache size has no effect on speed
blockMcqs.explanation: Capacity misses drop with size, but access time and cost per byte both rise, so gains diminish.

blockMcqs.question: Why might hardware skip true LRU?
options: LRU is illegal in modern chips
Tracking exact use order costs extra hardware
LRU always performs worse than random
LRU cannot be implemented in silicon
blockMcqs.explanation: Exact LRU needs per-set bookkeeping; pseudo-LRU or random often gets close enough more cheaply.
